# Getting Started

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(countdown)
library(tidycensus)
options(scipen=999)

opts_chunk$set(warning=FALSE, message=FALSE)

airbnb <- read_csv('https://bit.ly/3oadz2L', col_types = cols())
climate <- read_csv('https://bit.ly/3kKErEb', col_types = cols())
mba <- read_csv("https://bit.ly/4evYpeW", col_types = cols())

# Census chunks only run when a key is available (see census_api_key())
has_census_key <- nzchar(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"))
if (has_census_key) {
  wa_counties <- get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    state = "WA",
    variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001", population = "B01003_001"),
    year = 2024,
    output = "wide"
  )
}
```

---

# Set Up

- Set up your machine to run R
  - Install R [on a Mac with an Intel chip](https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/macosx/big-sur-x86_64/base/R-4.6.1-x86_64.pkg), [on a Mac with a silicon chip](https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/macosx/sonoma-arm64/base/R-4.6.1-arm64.pkg), or [on a PC](https://cloud.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/R-4.6.1-win.exe)
  - Install RStudio [on a Mac](https://download1.rstudio.org/electron/macos/RStudio-2026.09.0-174.dmg) or [on a PC](https://download1.rstudio.org/electron/windows/RStudio-2026.09.0-174.exe)
- Save a Census API key so R can pull Census data
  1. Request a free [Census API key](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html) and find it in your email
  2. Paste your key between the quotes below and run the code in the RStudio **Console** (not in a script)
  3. Restart R: **Session > Restart R**

```r
install.packages("tidycensus")
tidycensus::census_api_key("PASTE-YOUR-KEY-HERE", install = TRUE)
Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") # After restarting R, this should print your key
```

- OPTIONAL: Create a [Claude](https://claude.com/), [ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/), and/or [GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/features/copilot) account

# R and the R Programmer 

- Typical uses for R
  - Data preparation (cleaning, reshaping, creation)  
  - Data analysis
  - Data visualization
  - Modeling 
  - Productizing and automation
- Mental models and analysis tools
  - Excel/SPSS/Stata --> computational programming tools like R
- The typical R programmer
  - Leverages Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, or another AI assistant
  - Googles for answers
  - Borrows code
  - Asks friends and pros for help
- Useful references (see Reference Materials in the [syllabus](https://gbearden.github.io/r_course_evans_school/) for more)
  - help()
  - ??
  - [R Bloggers](https://www.r-bloggers.com/)
  - [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/r)
  
---

# AI Tools and R Programming

- R programmer AI tools
  - Browser-based tools (Claude, ChatGPT)  
  - Desktop AI assistant apps
  - Desktop AI-enabled code editors (VS Code)  
  - Statistical models (transformers, neural network models, GANs)  
  - Cloud-based Ops orchestration (auto-scaling cloud resources, incident detection)
- Common prompting strategies
  - Role Prompting (*“As if you were a lead data scientist with extensive experience building complex EHR data models [...]”*)
  - Ask for code and explanations
  - Be specific and mention specific tasks, libraries, and error messages
  - Iterate, clarifying if the first answer isn’t right
  - Break down tasks (*“First clean data, then summarize, then plot.”*)
  - Use XML tags (&lt;Tag1&gt;)

# Quick Tour of RStudio

- Script vs. notebook  
  - Scripts are good for code development, running code in production, version control, and multi-file analyses
  - Notebooks are good for sharing analysis, documentation, mixed code in a single file
- Run code from the notebook and the console

- Make sure you can install packages
  - Command line/Console
  - RStudio GUI

# <img src="figures/tools.png" style="height: 50px"/> Libraries, <span style='color:#6DA34D'>functions</span>, data

**Anatomy of a function**  

```r
compute_mean <- function(x) { 
  # Calculate the sum of all values in `x`
  x_sum <- sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # We'll learn more about the ! operator later
  # Just know that the code below used to create `x_clean` removes NA values
  x_clean <- x[!is.na(x)]
  
  # Count the number of values in `x`
  x_len <- length(x_clean)
  
  # Divide `x_sum` by `x_len`
  x_mean <- x_sum / x_len
  
  # `return` is used to tell R the output of the function
  return(x_mean)
  }
```

# <img src="figures/data.png" style="height: 50px"/> Libraries, functions, <span style='color:#6DA34D'>data</span>

- Knowing data types when programming is really important!
  - Creates a set of rules for what operations can be executed  
- Data types  
  - Vectors, data frames, tibbles
      - `str_subset()` removes a value from a string
      - `filter()` removes an observation from a data frame or tibble
  - Vectors
      - Integers, numbers, characters, factors
      - You can sum integers and numbers, but not character strings
      - You can make character strings upper case, but not integers and numbers
  
```r
starwars
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, collapse=FALSE}
head(starwars, 3)
```

---

# <img src="figures/data.png" style="height: 50px"/> Libraries, functions, <span style='color:#6DA34D'>data</span>

**More on data types**

- Inspect the dataset  
  - `class()` tells the overall type  
  - `is.[type]()` checks if something is numeric, character, etc.  
- Access parts of a dataset  
  - `$` to pull a column as a vector  
  - `[ ]` to pull elements by position  
- Create and coerce variables  
  - `as.character()`, `as.numeric()`  

**Import and inspect your own dataset with `read_csv()`**  

```r
byod_df <- read_csv("[...].csv")
# Or take a look at the 538 partisan lean dataset from 2022
# https://github.com/fivethirtyeight/data/tree/master/partisan-lean
byod_df <- read_csv("http://bit.ly/48Ru0Ip")
```

library(tidycensus)

wa_counties <- get_acs(

- Error that a key already exists? Re-run the set up code with `overwrite = TRUE` added, then restart R

# Base R functions to explore tibbles

---

# Base R functions to explore tibbles 

Get in the habit of running these functions when you open a new dataset

- `head()` shows you the top of a tibble (or data frame)
  - `head()` shows 6 rows by default  
  - `tail()` shows the bottom of a tibble  
  - `arrange()` pairs nicely with subsetting functions to explore your data
- `summary()` shows summary statistics on all variables in a dataset
  - Reported summary statistics depend on the variable type
  - Min, max, mean, and median are reported for numeric variables 
- `ls()` shows all variables in a tibble
  - You can also use `ls()` without calling an object between the parentheses to see all objects in your workspace
- `str()` tells the variable type and selected variable values in a tibble for all variables
- `dim()` tells you the dimensions of your dataset
  - `nrow()` reports the number of rows only 
  - `ncol()` reports the number of columns only

# Base R functions to explore vectors

- `table()` shows you the distribution of values in a vector  
  - Indexed by name and position  
- `length()` tells you the number of elements in a vector  
- `unique()` shows you the unique values in a vector  
- `sort()` orders values in a vector  
- `summary()` shows you descriptive statistics on a vector  
  - `summary()` can run on a vector or tibble  

--

You can nest multiple functions
```r
length(unique(wa_counties$NAME))
```

---

# Troubleshooting your R code

Make sure...

- You loaded your libraries
- Arguments in your functions are comma-separated
- Your functions have opening and closing parentheses
- You have start and end quotation marks where relevant
- The variable type is correct to perform the function you call
  - For example, you probably don't want to run `min()` on a character string
- Your assignment operator looks like this: `<-`
- You're running code inside a code chunk (in a notebook)

--

Feel free to ask an AI assistant why you see an error!

```
Why does this code throw an error in R? 
[Your code]
```
